questions.explanation: Next year's production is 25 million times 1.04, which is 26.0 million tonnes, and 500 divided by 26.0 is 19.23, so the ratio is 19.2 years. Written the other way the same figure is 20 divided by 1.04, since 500 over 25 is 20 years at a flat rate, and discounting one year of growth at 4 percent gives 19.23 again. The number to avoid is 20, which is what the ratio would be if output never grew, and the difference between 20 and 19.2 is the whole reason a company publishes which year the denominator comes from. A reserve-to-production ratio is also a statement about one year only: it says nothing about price, about resources that are known but not proved, or about reserves that a change in technology or in demand would never be produced.

Against an allocation of 0.40 cubic kilometres the share is 0.219 divided by 0.40, which is 0.5475, so 54.8 percent. Working in cubic metres throughout gives the same answer, because 0.40 cubic kilometres is 400 million cubic metres and 219 million over 400 million is 0.5475. The number to avoid is 150, which comes from dividing the allocation by the barrels rather than the demand by the allocation, and the size of the share is the point of the item: a method can meet the oil target and still be impossible in a basin that is already close to its water limit.

The base load is 40 percent of the peak, so the two numbers a planner has to hold at once are quite different, and that gap is the entire reason a system with intermittent sources needs storage, interconnection or dispatchable capacity sized against the peak rather than the average.

questions.explanation: The present value of a level saving over n years is the saving times the factor one minus 1.05 to the minus n, all divided by 0.05, and that factor has to reach 12 divided by 3, which is 4, so 1.05 to the minus n has to equal 0.8. Taking logarithms gives n as 0.2231 over 0.04879, which is 4.57 years. Summing the discounted years by hand gives the same result to within a rounding step: 2.857, 2.721, 2.592 and 2.468 million by the end of year four, 10.638 million in total, and the fifth year's 2.351 million takes the total past 12 million part way through. The lesson is that the discount rate lengthens the payback, so a project with a simple payback inside the financing horizon can still fail that test.

questions.explanation: The capital recovery factor turns 900 million into 900 times 0.1627, which is 146.43 million dollars a year, and adding the 22 million of fuel and operation gives 168.43 million a year. Since 120 GWh is 120 million kilowatt hours, the levelised cost is 168.43 million over 120 million, which is 1.404 dollars a kilowatt-hour. Splitting the two components gives the same figure, because the capital alone is 146.43 over 120, or 1.220, and the operating part is 22 over 120, or 0.183, and 1.220 plus 0.183 is 1.403. The capital term is 87 percent of the total, which is the usual result for a low-operating-cost plant and the reason the assumption about hours of use, which is embedded in the capital recovery factor, matters more than any efficiency figure quoted alongside it.

The same share can be found as a time: 20.75 GJ over 20 years is 1.0375 GJ a year of average input, and 0.75 divided by that is 0.72 years, which is 0.72 out of 20 years or 3.6 percent. The number to avoid is 3.75, which is 0.75 over 20 alone and so leaves the embodied energy out of the denominator; that is the ratio of embodied to operating alone, and the question asked for a share of the whole. For most appliances the embodied part is a small share, and for a building fabric it is not, which is the difference that makes life-cycle thinking necessary for one and optional for the other.

questions.explanation: At 5.0 global hectares a person, 800,000 residents are allocated 4.00 million global hectares of biocapacity, and a footprint of 1.20 million is well inside it, so the accounting reports a surplus of 2.80 million global hectares. The same figure comes from the per-person route, because 1.20 million over 800,000 is 1.5 global hectares a person against the 5.0 assumed, and 3.5 times 800,000 is again 2.80 million. The surplus is an artefact of the assumption rather than a fact about the city, because the average global hectare the method applies is a low-productivity hectare and the city is not living on the average one. A city in a rich country can therefore appear to hold a large share of the planet's capacity while its own residents' consumption, counted with the productivity of the land they actually use, exceeds what that land can supply.

questions.explanation: The two inventories differ by 5.6 minus 4.0, which is 1.6 million tonnes, and that difference is the net emissions embodied in imports, so 1.6 over 5.6 is 0.2857, that is 28.6 percent of the consumption-based total. Taking the complement gives the same answer, because 4.0 over 5.6 is 0.7143 and one minus that is 0.2857. The boundary is what decides the answer, since the same city reports two defensible numbers a long way apart and each is correct for its own question. A territorial inventory is the one a local government can influence with local rules, and a consumption-based inventory is the one that describes what the city's residents actually cause, so a policy that uses the first and claims to have addressed the second has changed the boundary instead of the emissions.

questions.explanation: Over 20 years gas X contributes 0.50 times 200, which is 100 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, and gas Y contributes 12 times 3, which is 36, so the total is 136. On the 100-year column the same leak is 0.50 times 40, which is 20, plus 36, which is 56. The two totals for the same emission differ by a factor of 2.4, and the whole of the difference comes from gas X, whose short-lived behaviour makes it far more powerful over 20 years and much less so over 100. That is why a factor is meaningless without its horizon, and why a target expressed as a single percentage over 50 years can be met while a 20-year policy on the same gases moves in the opposite direction.
questions.hint: Apply each factor to its own gas before adding the two, and use the 20-year column.

questions.explanation: At 400 firms the flat charge is 2.0 million over 400, which is 5,000 dollars, and at 250 firms the same 2.0 million gives 8,000. Scaling the first figure by the change in firm count confirms it, since 5,000 times 400 over 250 is 8,000. The two numbers together are the regulatory consequence, because a flat charge raises each remaining firm's cost by 60 percent at the same time as the sector is losing firms, and a rule whose fixed cost is recovered per firm therefore discourages precisely the consolidation that lowers average cost elsewhere. It also shrinks the base, so the total collected is unchanged while the number of firms paying falls, and the burden of the programme ends up concentrated on the ones left. Charging by output or by emissions instead spreads the fixed cost in proportion to the activity that creates the need to monitor it.
questions.hint: The programme cost is fixed, so divide the same cost by the smaller number of firms.
questions.learningObjective: compute a flat charge on a fixed programme cost as the sector shrinks

questions.explanation: After approval the region carries seven permits of 100 units, which is 700 units a year, and the assessment has examined only the 100 units of the application, so 600 units are outside it. Counting the six existing permits gives the same figure directly. A different way to see the gap is as a share, since 600 over 700 is 86 percent of the regional load, so the assessment addresses an eighth of what will be emitted there. The reason it comes out that way is structural rather than careless: a single-project assessment is required to compare the project with the no-action alternative, not with the other six projects, and nobody in the room is representing their permits. A regional cap is the instrument that fills the gap, because it is the only thing that makes the six existing permits comparable with the seventh.

questions.explanation: Intensity is waste divided by output, so start from 100 tonnes of waste and 100 tonnes of product, where the intensity is 1.00. After the year there are 70 tonnes of waste and 120 tonnes of product, so the intensity is 70 over 120, which is 0.583, and that is a 41.7 percent improvement. Reading it as a ratio of the two changes gives the same figure, because 0.70 divided by 1.20 is 0.583. The number to avoid is 30, which is the fall in the waste and is the figure the report leads with, and the reason it is wrong is that the output rose while the waste fell, so the same waste is spread over more product. The indicator cannot see the plant in the next region, which now handles part of that output and appears in neither the numerator nor the denominator.
questions.hint: An intensity is a ratio, so take the change in the waste and divide by the change in the output.

questions.explanation: Container glass is 30,000 tonnes of the recovered material out of the 50,000 tonnes the survey found in the collected refuse, so the rate for that material is 30,000 over 50,000, which is 0.60, that is 60 percent. The overall rate for comparison is 120,000 over 480,000, which is 25 percent, so the glass rate is two and a half times the headline. The distinction matters in both directions, because a single headline rate can be depressed by a large low-recycling stream such as food or textiles while the material a city has actually targeted does far better than the headline suggests, and it can equally be propped up by one stream that happens to be easy while a targeted material is being neglected. questions.explanation: Before the income falls the charge is 400 over 40,000, which is 1.00 percent, and afterwards it is 400 over 38,000, which is 1.0526 percent, so 1.05 percent. Comparing the two shares gives the same result, because 1.0526 divided by 1.00 is 1.0526, so the burden has risen about 5.3 percent in relative terms even though the household pays the same 400 dollars. Nothing about the price has changed; the household's position has. That is the whole argument about a price whose revenue is returned in equal amounts rather than in proportion to the charge, and it is why an equal rebate neutralises the charge for the median payer and still leaves the households below the median paying a larger share of what they have. The remedy is to make the return progressive rather than to argue that the charge is not there.

Auctioning is what makes a revenue stream of this kind available at all, because free allocation sends the value of the allowances to the firms that hold them, and the size of the transfer is the difference between those two designs. The equal payment is a per-person rebate of the charge, which is why it leaves the households below the median paying a larger share of their income than before.

questions.explanation: The new price is 20 times 1.10, which is 22 dollars, and the new quantity is 100 million times 0.94, which is 94 million units, so the revenue is 22 times 94 million, or 2,068 million dollars. Scaling the original revenue by the two changes gives the same figure, because 2,000 times 1.10 times 0.94 is 2,068, which is a 3.4 percent rise. The quantity response has to be smaller than the price rise for the revenue to rise, and 6 percent against 10 percent is exactly that case, so the tax is not self-defeating here even though it is not a large behavioural response either. The number to watch is the elasticity, because once the quantity fall reaches the price rise the revenue has peaked and every further rise in the price reduces it, which is the point at which a tax on fuel stops being a revenue instrument and becomes purely a signal.

questions.explanation: The distinction is between what is held and what is moving, and it decides every question that follows. A stock is a quantity in a reservoir at a moment, so it can be unchanged over a day or a year while the flows through it are large, and it is stocks that determine how long a resource lasts at any given rate of use. A flow is a rate of transfer between reservoirs, and adding or subtracting it is what changes a stock. The atmospheric burden is a stock, so it responds to the balance of all the flows into and out of the atmosphere, which is why an emission figure and a concentration figure answer different questions and why a policy stated only in flows can still leave the stock rising for a long time.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two numbers could stay the same while the other changes.

questions.explanation: Renewable and non-renewable describe a rate and a stock, not a substance, and the test is whether the stock is being drawn down. Wood is a renewable resource when it is harvested at or below the rate at which the stand regrows, and it is a depletable resource in the district that is cutting faster than the stand can replace, because the standing stock falls every year and the harvest has to be financed from the stock until the cutting stops. The same test applies to fisheries, to groundwater and to grassland, and in each case a resource that is being used faster than it regenerates is being converted from a flow into a stock without anyone deciding to change the classification. That is the error behind a great many official accounts of a supposedly renewable sector.

questions.explanation: A reserve-to-production ratio is a stock divided by a single year's rate, and the two halves move for reasons that have nothing to do with each other. Production responds to price, to technology, to policy and to demand, so a ratio computed at a low price can double in a few years as production rises, and it can equally collapse if the same price destroys the industry that was producing at that rate. The ratio also counts only proved reserves, and what counts as proved depends on price assumptions that are not published with the number. A ratio of 30 is therefore a statement about a world in which price, demand and policy stay where they are, which is the assumption a security claim rests on and the assumption that has to be stated when one is made.

questions.explanation: An intermittent source supplies energy rather than guaranteed power, and the gap between the two is the whole of the balancing problem. A quarter of annual generation can coexist with almost no output on a winter evening, so a system with that share has to be able to meet its peak for a run of dark hours, and that capability has to come from somewhere: storage, interconnection with a neighbour that is generating, or plant that can be held back for those hours. Adding more of the same source does not fix the dark hours, and dividing annual energy by peak demand does not create capacity that can be called on at six in the evening. The consequence for a plan is that the cost of a high renewable share is set by the balancing requirement, and a comparison of costs that leaves that out is comparing a nameplate with a delivered service.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be available during the hours when the resource is producing nothing.

questions.explanation: A levelised cost prices energy as though every kilowatt-hour were interchangeable, and they are not, because a kilowatt-hour delivered into a system with a shortage at six in the evening is worth more than one delivered at noon into a system with surplus. The division also commits the report to assumptions about hours of operation, the discount rate and the plant's life that are embedded in the capital recovery factor and are not visible in the number. None of that makes the figure wrong for what it does measure, and it remains a fair way to rank two options on cost per unit of energy; what it cannot do is settle a question about a system, where timing, capacity and interconnection are what the decision turns on. The omitted terms are also the ones that differ most between the options, which is why a cost ranking can be right and still pick the wrong one.
questions.hint: Ask what the division assumes about one kilowatt-hour and any other.

questions.explanation: The timing is the whole difficulty. questions.explanation: The fee is a function of tonnage alone, and a default factor supplies the emissions number for every site, so two sites with the same waste and completely different capture records are charged identically. The site capturing 11 percent is emitting several times what the site capturing 62 percent is, and the liability is priced as though they were the same, so the instrument taxes the tonnage rather than the damage. That is the general weakness of any charge built on a default where the quantity being priced is not the thing being measured, and it gets worse as the difference between sites grows. The design is defensible for a charge that exists to cover an administrative cost, because then tonnage is the right base, and indefensible for a charge that exists to internalise an externality, because there the emissions have to be measured, estimated site by site, or the charge is a signal with no relation to the harm it names.

Under those conditions the ratio is a fair comparison, and it is a genuinely useful one because it puts a capital cost and a fuel cost on a single scale that a reader can check. It points at the wrong thing when the options differ in anything the division cannot see. It prices a kilowatt-hour at noon the same as one at the evening peak, which understates the value of the resource that can deliver in the short run and the cost of a plant that is needed only for a few hours. It commits to an hours-of-use figure inside the capital recovery factor, so a plant that will run less is flattered. answer.ex: The two targets are measured on different sides of the same transaction. An efficiency target divides energy by service, so it rewards whatever makes the service cheaper to deliver: better fabric, a more efficient appliance, a cheaper fuel. It is the right target when the aim is to remove waste, because the waste is exactly the difference between the two sides, and it gives a manufacturer and a builder a clear thing to improve. It is the wrong target for the amount of service people get, because a cheaper service is bought in greater quantity: a warmer building, a longer shower, a second machine, a delivery that replaces a trip, and the efficiency of the equipment improves while the total goes up. A service target, in joules delivered or in the temperature maintained, holds the quantity still and lets the price do its work, so the saving shows up in the bill rather than in the use. Running the two together is the strongest design, because the first makes the service cheaper to supply and the second stops the saving being spent on more of it, and reporting only the first is what makes an efficiency programme look like it has solved a demand problem.

answer.ex: A life-cycle result is an integration over a boundary, so two studies differ whenever their boundaries differ, and nothing about the arithmetic requires them to agree. One may stop at the factory gate, counting feedstock extraction, manufacturing and the waste leaving the site; the other may run to the end of life and add the use phase, which for a product that consumes energy in use is often the largest single term, together with the impacts of disposal. A third may sit between them by excluding capital goods or by using a different allocation rule for a shared process, and allocation is itself a choice with a large effect whenever a process makes several products. The stages left out do not stop contributing when they are left out, so a narrower boundary produces a smaller number and nothing more. To compare the two studies, three things have to be made identical and stated: the functional unit, which is what the figure is per, the boundary, and the allocation rule for any shared process. Once those match, a remaining difference is a real difference and worth investigating; before they match, a difference is not evidence of anything.

questions.explanation: Excluded stages keep contributing, so a narrower boundary is a smaller number and not a different measurement.
questions.hint: Ask what each study counted, and whether the excluded stages stopped contributing.
questions.learningObjective: explain how a boundary makes a life-cycle result question-specific

answer.ex: The engineering work is bounded and estimable: a facility is designed to a standard, the quantity of material to be placed, the drainage to be built and the monitoring to be run, and a competent designer can put a defensible number on it. The financial structure is harder, because the work falls due over decades, after the revenue that could pay for it has ended, and the operator that incurred the liability may by then have been acquired, sold its assets, or closed entirely, in which case an unsecured promise from a company that no longer exists is worth nothing to whoever has to carry the cost. Setting the money aside while the mine is still operating is the only point at which the operator still has a reason to provide it, and converting that obligation into a bond or a dedicated fund turns a future promise into a present asset that can be drawn down. The second-order problem follows from the first, because the estimate of a closure cost is revised upwards as survey work and monitoring replace desk assumptions, so an instrument sized against the first estimate decays in value and has to be tied to the estimate rather than set once.

questions.explanation: The work is estimable but the payer is not, so the money has to be committed while there is still a reason to commit it.
questions.hint: Ask who will still exist, and who will hold the money, on the date the work falls due.
questions.learningObjective: explain why post-closure liability is a financial problem before it is an engineering one

questions.explanation: The period opens with a published cap, because the number of allowances is what the cap fixes and nothing else in the scheme works until that number exists and is issued. Emissions are then reported and verified, and the verification matters because a surrender obligation based on an unchecked report is a self-assessment, and the whole design depends on the report being the number the regulator is willing to act on. Only then can the surrender obligation be discharged, by handing over one allowance for each tonne or by buying what it does not hold at whatever the market price has become. The unused allowances are traded or banked last, since a holder can only know what it will not need once it knows what it emitted, and banking is what allows a firm to cut sharply in one year and stay within its obligations in the next.
questions.hint: Nothing can be reported before the allowances exist, and nothing is surrendered before the report.

Each installation must hold one allowance for every tonne it emitted, buying any it lacks
Allowances it does not need are sold to another holder or banked for a later period

questions.explanation: Design comes first, because the ability to separate parts without damaging them is fixed when the product is made and no later step can create it, which is the reason a product designed to be glued together can never enter a loop however willing its user is. Collection is second, since a separated product that stays in the household's general refuse is not in the loop at all. Sorting is third, and it is the step that splits the stream: components that can be reused whole go back into service, which is the better outcome because it avoids the energy of reprocessing, and only the rest goes on. Reprocessing is last, and it is the step that actually closes the loop, because a material only returns to the productive stock when it goes back into manufacturing as a raw material. Calling a scheme circular on the strength of its collection rate alone mistakes the second step for the fourth.
questions.hint: Nothing can be returned that was never brought back or cannot be taken apart.

options.text: The product is designed so its parts can be separated without being destroyed in the process
The product is collected from where it was used rather than discarded with general refuse
Its components are sorted, and those that can be reused whole are put straight back into service
The remaining material is reprocessed and returns to manufacturing as a raw material

questions.explanation: Screening comes first because it is the cheapest possible question and it prevents the whole process being spent on a proposal that a threshold would have excluded, or on one that a later stage would have approved without the study. Scoping follows, and it is the stage that does the most damage to a project that has already fixed its design, because it sets the boundary and it names the alternatives, and both of those decide what the study can conclude. The description and prediction of effects come third, and they are the part of the assessment that is quoted as though it were the whole, when the comparison of options is what actually determines the outcome. Design of mitigation and the decision come last, and by then the option has been chosen, so a condition attached at this stage can shape how the project is built but not whether it is built.
questions.hint: The cheapest question comes first and the choice of what to compare has to precede the comparison.

questions.explanation: Avoidance comes first because it removes the material before any of the later steps has to deal with it, and no recovery process can be as good as not generating the waste, which is why the cheapest tonne of waste is the one that was never produced. Reuse is second, and it is better than recycling the same material because a part that goes back into service keeps the energy of manufacture as well as the substance, whereas recycling has to reprocess the material and lose most of that energy. Recycling is third and is the only one of the four that returns the material to the productive stock, so it is the step that actually closes a loop. Energy recovery is last of these four, and it is a disposal route dressed as a recovery: carbon leaves the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, the material cannot be reused, and a concentrated residue still has to be placed. Disposal sits below all of them, and a waste hierarchy is a ranking in which each step down is worse rather than merely different.
questions.hint: Ask which option keeps the most material out of a residual stream, and which one still produces one.

The material is reprocessed and returned to manufacturing as a raw material
Energy is recovered from what is left, which still leaves a residue to be placed somewhere
